title: Two Characters
directAnswer: Delete every character except two chosen distinct letters, and the survivor must alternate (no two adjacent equal) — find the longest such string. For each unordered pair of distinct letters present in s, keep only those two letters and check the filtered string alternates; if it does, its length is a candidate. Return the max candidate, or 0 if none qualifies. With alphabet size k ≤ 26, that's O(k² · n) — for lowercase letters, effectively O(n).

rules: You may delete **all** occurrences of any letter, but the survivors must be exactly **two distinct** letters.
'Valid' means the kept string **alternates** — `t[i] != t[i+1]` everywhere.
A valid alternating string of two letters automatically has length ≥ 2; if no pair alternates, answer is **0**.
Only consider letters that actually appear — pairing with an absent letter wastes work.
Filtering preserves original order; never reorder the survivors.
whenToUse: Restrict a string to a small fixed set of allowed symbols and test a local property
The alphabet is tiny (≤ 26) so enumerating pairs is cheap
You need the longest subsequence using exactly two symbols with an adjacency rule
Deleting whole character classes (all of a letter) is permitted
antiSignals: Any number of distinct letters allowed → not this pairwise enumeration
Deletions are limited / costed → becomes a DP, not free filtering
Subarray (contiguous) required, not subsequence → sliding window instead
Huge alphabet (k large) → O(k²·n) pair enumeration is too slow
remember.takeaway: Because the answer uses only two distinct letters, you can brute-force over the ≤ 325 letter pairs, filter the string to each pair, and keep the longest one that alternates. Tiny alphabet turns an apparently exponential 'choose a subsequence' problem into a quadratic-in-alphabet scan.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you exploit the 'exactly two distinct letters' constraint to bound the search to letter pairs instead of all subsequences, and whether you correctly define 'valid' as strict alternation after filtering.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Trying to build the answer greedily in one pass, or forgetting that a pair which produces adjacent duplicates (like 'aa') after filtering must be rejected entirely — not just trimmed.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Point out the alphabet bound: there are at most C(26,2)=325 pairs, so enumerating pairs and filtering is O(k²·n), and that 'valid' reduces to a single adjacency scan per pair.

problemStatement:
You are given a string `s`. You may delete **all** occurrences of one or more characters (i.e. remove entire letters). After deletions, the resulting string `t` is **valid** if:

1. `t` contains **exactly two distinct characters**, and
2. no two adjacent characters of `t` are the same (it alternates, e.g. `"ababab"`).

Return the length of the **longest** valid string obtainable, or `0` if no such string exists.
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters
You may delete every occurrence of any chosen letters
The kept string must alternate between exactly two distinct letters
understanding: Picture the final string: it uses just two letters, x and y, and reads x y x y … (or y x y x …). Because deleting is free and order is preserved, the best string for a chosen pair {x, y} is simply s with every other letter removed. That filtered string is valid only if it already alternates — if filtering leaves two of the same letter adjacent, that pair is impossible. Try all pairs, keep the longest valid result.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can I keep just one letter?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No. A valid string needs exactly two distinct characters. A single-letter result doesn't qualify.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Does deleting mean removing some or all of a letter?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: All occurrences of the letters you don't keep. You can't selectively keep some 'a's and drop others — it's all-or-nothing per letter.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What if no pair alternates?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Return 0. For example "aaa" or "beeb" filtered to any pair leaves adjacent duplicates.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is order preserved?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. Filtering keeps the original relative order; you never rearrange characters.

approaches.whenToMention: Mention only to frame the search space, then immediately reject it — it's exponential and impractical past tiny n.

approaches.complexityReasoning: There are 2ⁿ subsequences, and validating each costs O(n) → O(2ⁿ · n). Hopeless beyond n ≈ 20.
approaches.explanation:
The most literal interpretation: a valid string is some subsequence of `s`, so enumerate every subsequence and test the two conditions (exactly two distinct letters, strictly alternating), tracking the longest valid one.

**Why it's correct.** It examines every possible deletion outcome, so it cannot miss the optimum.

**Why it's unusable.** With `n` up to 1000 there are `2¹⁰⁰⁰` subsequences — astronomically more than atoms in the universe. The point of stating it is to surface the key realization: the answer is constrained to **two distinct letters**, and once you fix which two, the best subsequence is forced (keep both letters, drop the rest). That collapses `2ⁿ` choices into one per letter pair.
approaches.insight: When a brute force is exponential but the answer is restricted to a tiny structure (here: two letters), enumerate the structure, not the raw choices. Fixing the two letters removes all freedom — you must keep every occurrence of both — so there's nothing left to search inside a pair.

approaches.name: Enumerate Letter Pairs and Filter (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The intended answer — frame as 'fix the two letters, keep only them, check it alternates'.
hints: The result uses exactly two distinct letters. How many such pairs are possible over a 26-letter alphabet?

approaches.complexityReasoning: There are at most C(k,2) ≤ 325 letter pairs. Filtering and the alternation check are each O(n). Total O(k² · n); for lowercase letters k ≤ 26 so this is effectively linear in n with a constant factor.
approaches.explanation:
Collect the distinct letters of `s`. For every unordered pair `{x, y}`, build the filtered string keeping only `x` and `y` in their original order. The filtered string is valid iff no two adjacent characters are equal; if valid, its length is a candidate. Return the largest candidate, or 0.

**Why fixing the pair removes all choice.** Once you commit to letters `x` and `y`, deleting is mandatory for every other letter and forbidden for `x`/`y` (deleting an occurrence could only shorten or break alternation, never help). So the unique best subsequence for that pair is the full filtered string — there's nothing to optimize within a pair.

**Why the alternation check is a simple adjacency scan.** After filtering, the only failure mode is two of the same letter sitting next to each other (which happens when the original had `…x x…` with nothing of `y` between them). Scanning neighbours catches exactly that. If it survives, the string already alternates `x y x y …`.

**Why reject, not trim.** If `"aabab"` filters to `"aabab"` with a leading `aa`, you can't just drop one `a` — you committed to keeping all of `x` and `y`. So a duplicate adjacency disqualifies the whole pair; you don't salvage a prefix.

**Why the alphabet bound makes this fast.** At most 325 pairs, each costing O(n), is trivially within limits for `n ≤ 1000`.
approaches.insight: The 'exactly two letters' rule is a search-space cap in disguise: instead of choosing among 2ⁿ subsequences, you choose among ≤ 325 letter pairs, and each pair has a single forced answer. Spotting a small fixed alphabet and turning it into the outer loop is the reusable trick.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Trimming instead of rejecting
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Once you keep letters x and y, you keep ALL of them. If filtering leaves 'aa' adjacent, the pair is simply invalid — you can't drop one 'a' to fix it, because that violates 'delete all or none of a letter'.

patternNote: Small-alphabet enumeration. When the answer is confined to a tiny fixed structure (here, exactly two letters from a 26-letter alphabet), enumerate that structure as the outer loop and let each choice force the rest. Turns an exponential subsequence search into O(k²·n).
